title: Parliament’s Monsoon Session Opens With Seven Bills and the Delimitation Question
excerpt: The government has listed five new bills and two pending ones for the session running July 20 to August 13, but the politically explosive delimitation proposal remains conspicuously absent from the official agenda.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Parliament's Monsoon Session runs from July 20 to August 13, with 19 sittings scheduled.
  • Seven bills are on the agenda, including taxation reform and MSME development.
  • The contentious delimitation bill is absent but may still be introduced unexpectedly.
  • NDA's strength has increased to 318 Lok Sabha members, but still short of a two-thirds majority.
  • Opposition dynamics are strained, with the DMK requesting separate seating from Congress.

  • Parliament’s Monsoon Session opens July 20 and runs through August 13, with 19 scheduled sittings.
  • The government has listed seven bills — five new and two pending — covering taxation, Supreme Court expansion, MSME reform and national honour protections.
  • The politically charged delimitation bill is absent from the official agenda but could still be introduced during the session under constitutional provisions.
  • The NDA’s strength has grown since April through defections from the TMC and other parties, though it still falls short of the two-thirds majority needed for the constitutional amendment.

The Official Agenda

India’s Parliament begins its Monsoon Session on July 20, with the government listing seven bills for a session that runs through August 13 across 19 sittings. The agenda spans taxation reform, judicial expansion and business regulation — but it is what is missing that has drawn the most attention.

Among the five new bills, the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill, 2026, replaces an ordinance aimed at deepening India’s sovereign debt market and attracting global capital amid geopolitical turbulence. The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill proposes increasing the court’s sanctioned strength from 33 to 37 judges, excluding the Chief Justice.

Three other proposals round out the new legislation: a Registration of Births and Deaths amendment, the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill — which would criminalise insults to Vande Mataram — and the MSME Development (Amendment) Bill, aimed at modernising the regulatory framework for small businesses.

The Delimitation Shadow

The government’s most ambitious legislative project — the 131st Constitution Amendment Bill, which would expand the Lok Sabha from 550 to 850 seats through delimitation — is conspicuously absent from the official programme. In April, the bill fell 54 votes short of the required two-thirds majority, with the government securing 298 votes against 230 in opposition.

But its omission from the agenda does not rule out a surprise. Under Article 368 of the Constitution, a Constitutional Amendment Bill can be introduced by any minister without prior notice or presidential approval. Reports suggest BJP leaders have been in contact with DMK chief M.K. Stalin and other regional leaders to expand support.

Shifting Parliamentary Arithmetic

The NDA’s numbers have strengthened since April. Twenty Lok Sabha MPs, including TMC leader Kakoli Ghosh Dastidar, joined the NDA-backed Nationalist Citizen Party in June, while six Shiv Sena (Uddhav) MPs merged with the Shinde faction. The NDA now counts 318 Lok Sabha members — up from 292 after the 2024 elections, but still 42 votes short of the two-thirds mark if all 540 current members vote.

In the Rajya Sabha, the NDA’s strength has risen to 149, with three TMC members joining the BJP in July and by-elections for their seats scheduled for July 24. Even with expected gains, the coalition would remain about 12 votes short in the upper house.

Opposition Dynamics

Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla chaired a Business Advisory Committee meeting on July 19, urging all parties to ensure “constructive deliberations.” But fissures within the opposition complicate matters. The DMK has requested separate seating from Congress in the Lok Sabha following Congress’s alliance with the TVK in Tamil Nadu, a public sign of strain within the INDIA bloc.

The Sonam Wangchuk issue — the climate activist has been on a hunger strike demanding Ladakh’s inclusion under the Sixth Schedule — is expected to feature prominently in opposition strategy during the session.

What NRIs Should Watch

The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, pending since March, could change how overseas donations to Indian NGOs and institutions are regulated — a matter of direct relevance to diaspora philanthropy. The income tax amendment may affect NRI investment flows, and the delimitation debate carries implications for political representation in states with large diaspora populations.

The session’s 19 sittings will determine whether the government can advance its legislative agenda or whether the opposition can force the accountability debates it is seeking on everything from Ladakh policy to the West Asia conflict’s impact on Indian citizens abroad.
